title: Content in all things (Philippians 4:10–23)
hook: I have learned to be content with little or plenty

segments.voice: Yesterday, a list of whatever is lovely, and your line was think on these things.

A package arrives at a prison. Inside, maybe money, maybe food, maybe a warm cloak, sent a long way by friends who scraped it together. The man who opens it has been cold and hungry before, and he's been comfortable, too. Now he sits down to write a thank-you note. The last stretch of Philippians is partly that note, for a gift carried by Epaphroditus. But Paul, being Paul, can't just say thanks. He has to explain something he's learned, and it's as practical as anything in the letter.

He's glad for the gift, and almost in the same breath says he wasn't desperate for it. In the King James Bible: "for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned. It didn't come naturally. Then: "I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need." Two things stand out. First, plenty is on the list. Contentment isn't only coping with too little. It's also not being owned by too much. Second, the word for instructed is unusual, a word used for being initiated into a secret, the way people were initiated into the mystery cults of the day. I've been let in on the secret, Paul says. And the secret is the next line, often quoted on its own: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." Read in its place, it isn't about winning a game or acing a test. It's about being hungry or full and staying steady either way. The word for content has a history too. Philosophers of Paul's day, the Stoics among them, prized it: being self-sufficient, needing nothing outside yourself. Paul shifts its center. Not self-sufficient. Sufficient in Christ. Then he thanks them warmly anyway, calls their gift "an odour of a sweet smell," and promises that God will supply all their need. The letter closes with greetings, even from people of Caesar's household. Philippians ends where it began: with joy, and with friends.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE LEARNED TO BE CONTENT.`

segments.voice: Look around you and name five things you already have, a chair, a window, a cup, a coat, your hands, without ranking them or wishing any were better; let each be enough for this minute. Then notice one want that keeps tugging at you, a thing to buy or to get, and let it sit there without obeying it. If you pray, you can give thanks for what's already here.
Contentment. Steadiness in plenty and in need. For Paul, it's learned, and it rests not on himself but on Christ who strengthens him.
Your line: I have learned contentment. Hungry or full, steady. That's Philippians, finished.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Philippians 4:11–13 in hard seasons and in seasons of plenty, and memorize the line about doing all things through Christ.

notes: The carry 'I have learned contentment' is a summary of 4:11; the KJV reads 'I have learned ... therewith to be content'.
μεμύημαι (4:12), 'I am instructed', linked to initiation into mystery cults: standard lexical note; confirm.
αὐτάρκης (4:11) as a Stoic ideal: standard; confirm.
The hook's description of the gift (money, food, a cloak) is illustrative; the letter doesn't specify. Hedged with 'maybe'. Confirm.
'Caesar's household' (4:22) likely means imperial servants or officials, not the emperor's family; the script does not specify.
